cards.title: Single-Threaded Event Loop & I/O Multiplexing
cards.question: Explain Single-Threaded Event Loop & I/O Multiplexing
cards.answer_30s: Redis executes commands on a single main thread using an I/O multiplexed event loop (epoll/kqueue) entirely in RAM, avoiding lock contention and thread context switches. Redis 6+ added multi-threaded socket I/O for parsing/writing network payloads while keeping command execution atomic.

code.body:
redis-cli INFO stats
redis-cli SLOWLOG GET 10

cards.typical_use: Achieving 100k+ ops/sec with sub-millisecond p99 latency.
pitfalls: Because command execution is single-threaded, O(N) commands like KEYS * or huge HGETALL block every client—use SCAN, HSCAN, and pagination.

cards.title: Core Data Structures (Strings, Hashes, ZSets, HyperLogLog, Streams)
cards.question: Explain Core Data Structures (Strings, Hashes, ZSets, HyperLogLog, Streams)
cards.answer_30s: Redis goes far beyond key-value strings: Hashes store objects compactly; Lists/Streams power queues; Sets handle unique tags; Sorted Sets (ZSet, skip list + hash table) rank items in O(log N); HyperLogLog estimates cardinality in 12KB.

code.body:
ZADD leaderboard 2450 "user:42"
ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 9 WITHSCORES
PFADD daily_uv:2026-11-25 "user:42"

cards.typical_use: Real-time leaderboards, sliding-window rate limiters, and unique visitor counting.
pitfalls: Know that Sorted Sets are backed by a skip list + hash table, giving O(log N) range queries and O(1) score lookups.

cards.title: Caching Patterns: Cache-Aside, Write-Through, Write-Behind
cards.question: Explain Caching Patterns: Cache-Aside, Write-Through, Write-Behind
cards.answer_30s: In Cache-Aside (lazy loading), the app checks Redis first, falls back to DB on miss, and populates Redis with a TTL. Write-Through updates cache and DB synchronously (consistent, slower writes). Write-Behind buffers writes in cache and flushes asynchronously to DB (fast writes, risk of data loss).
cards.typical_use: Cutting database read load by 80-95% in read-heavy APIs.
pitfalls: Always set TTLs with slight random jitter so keys don't expire simultaneously.

cards.title: Persistence: RDB Snapshots vs AOF (Append-Only File)
cards.question: Explain Persistence: RDB Snapshots vs AOF (Append-Only File)
cards.answer_30s: RDB forks a child process to write compact point-in-time binary snapshots (fast restarts, potential minutes of data loss). AOF logs every write command (with appendfsync everysec losing at most ~1s). Production deployments typically enable both RDB + AOF.

code.body:
# redis.conf
save 900 1
appendonly yes
appendfsync everysec

cards.typical_use: Balancing sub-millisecond write speed with durable crash recovery.
pitfalls: BGSAVE and BGREWRITEAOF use OS copy-on-write fork(); ensure host has sufficient RAM headroom during heavy writes.

cards.title: Distributed Locks, Atomic Lua Scripts & SET NX PX
cards.question: Explain Distributed Locks, Atomic Lua Scripts & SET NX PX
cards.answer_30s: Redis executes Lua scripts atomically as a single unit. A safe distributed lock uses `SET key token NX PX 10000` (atomic set-if-not-exists with expiry) and releases via a Lua script that verifies the caller's unique token before calling DEL.

code.body:
-- Safe lock release in Lua
if redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call('del', KEYS[1])
else
  return 0
end

cards.typical_use: Preventing duplicate cron jobs, payment double-charges, and distributed race conditions.
pitfalls: Explain why checking token before DEL matters: if GC paused Client A past TTL, Client B acquired the lock, and Client A must not delete B's lock.

cards.title: Eviction Policies (LRU, LFU) & Memory Limits
cards.question: Explain Eviction Policies (LRU, LFU) & Memory Limits
cards.answer_30s: When memory hits `maxmemory`, Redis applies `maxmemory-policy`: `allkeys-lru` evicts least recently used keys, `allkeys-lfu` evicts least frequently used keys (best for skewed hot-key caches), `volatile-ttl` evicts expiring keys first, and `noeviction` errors on writes.

code.body:
CONFIG SET maxmemory 4gb
CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lfu

cards.typical_use: Keeping Redis caches stable without OOM crashes.
pitfalls: For pure caches, prefer allkeys-lfu or allkeys-lru; for queues/session stores where data loss isn't acceptable, use noeviction + alerts.

cards.title: High Availability: Replication, Sentinel & Redis Cluster
cards.question: Explain High Availability: Replication, Sentinel & Redis Cluster
cards.answer_30s: Primary-replica replication scales reads asynchronously. Redis Sentinel monitors primaries and performs automated quorum-based failover. Redis Cluster shards data horizontally across 16,384 hash slots (`CRC16(key) % 16384`) across multiple primaries.

code.body:
# Hash tags force related keys onto the same cluster slot
SET user:{42}:profile "..."
SET user:{42}:prefs "..."

cards.typical_use: Scaling beyond single-node RAM limits and surviving node failures.
pitfalls: Multi-key commands (MGET, Lua scripts) fail across different Cluster slots unless you group keys with `{hash_tag}`.

cards.title: Pipelining & Rate Limiting Patterns
cards.question: Explain Pipelining & Rate Limiting Patterns
cards.answer_30s: Pipelining batches multiple commands into a single TCP round-trip, avoiding N network RTTs. Sliding-window or token-bucket rate limiters combine ZSet/Hash operations inside atomic Lua scripts.

code.body:
pipe = r.pipeline(transaction=False)
for uid in user_ids:
    pipe.get(f'user:{uid}')
results = pipe.execute()

cards.typical_use: Fetching 500 cached items in 1ms instead of 50ms of sequential RTTs.
pitfalls: Distinguish pipeline (batches network RTTs) from MULTI/EXEC (queues commands for atomic execution).

cards.title: ACLs, TLS & Network Isolation
cards.question: Explain ACLs, TLS & Network Isolation
cards.answer_30s: Never expose Redis to the public internet. Bind to private VPC subnets, require TLS in transit, disable/rename dangerous commands (`FLUSHALL`, `CONFIG`) via Redis 6+ ACLs, and enforce per-service least-privilege users.
cards.typical_use: Hardening production cache clusters against unauthorized data exfiltration.
pitfalls: Note that Redis's extreme speed means brute-forcing weak passwords is trivial—use high-entropy passwords and ACLs.

cards.title: Q: What are Cache Stampede, Cache Penetration, and Cache Avalanche?
cards.question: Q: What are Cache Stampede, Cache Penetration, and Cache Avalanche?
cards.answer_30s: A: Stampede (Thundering Herd): one hot key expires and 1,000 requests hit the DB simultaneously—fix with singleflight/mutex locks or probabilistic early refresh. Penetration: requests for non-existent IDs bypass cache repeatedly—fix with Bloom filters or caching short-TTL null markers. Avalanche: many keys expire at once or Redis crashes—fix with randomized TTL jitter and circuit breakers.

code.body: ttl = 3600 + random.randint(0, 300)  # Jitter prevents cache avalanche

cards.typical_use: One of the most frequently asked caching system design questions.
pitfalls: Covering all three failure modes clearly with their exact mitigations is an instant senior-level signal.

cards.title: Q: Why is Redis fast despite being single-threaded?
cards.question: Q: Why is Redis fast despite being single-threaded?
cards.answer_30s: A: 1) Data lives in RAM (nanosecond access vs millisecond disk). 2) Single-threaded execution avoids mutexes, deadlocks, and OS thread context switching. 3) Non-blocking I/O multiplexing (epoll/kqueue) handles tens of thousands of sockets efficiently. 4) Specialized C data structures (ziplist/listpack, skip list).
pitfalls: Contrast with Memcached (multi-threaded, simple key-value only, no persistence or rich data types).

cards.title: Q: How do you keep Redis and PostgreSQL consistent on writes?
cards.question: Q: How do you keep Redis and PostgreSQL consistent on writes?
cards.answer_30s: A: Prefer updating the DB first and then deleting (invalidating) the cache key rather than updating the cache, preventing concurrent write races from leaving stale values. For strict consistency, use outbox/CDC (Debezium) to invalidate cache asynchronously on committed WAL events.

code.body:
db.update_user(uid, data)
r.delete(f'user:{uid}')  # Invalidate rather than set

cards.typical_use: Preventing stale cache bugs under concurrent updates.
pitfalls: Mention the Cache-Aside race condition and why short TTLs act as a safety net.

cards.title: Q: Pub/Sub vs Redis Streams — which should you use for messaging?
cards.question: Q: Pub/Sub vs Redis Streams — which should you use for messaging?
cards.answer_30s: A: Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget with no persistence, no consumer groups, and dropped messages if a subscriber disconnects. Redis Streams is an append-only persistent log with consumer groups, message IDs, ACKs (XACK), and pending-entry recovery—use Streams for reliable queues and Pub/Sub only for ephemeral live broadcasts.

code.body:
XADD events * type order_created id 42
XREADGROUP GROUP workers w1 COUNT 10 STREAMS events >

cards.typical_use: Choosing the right Redis messaging primitive.
pitfalls: Compare Redis Streams with Kafka: Streams fits lightweight/medium throughput when Redis is already in stack; Kafka fits massive multi-TB durable logs.

cards.title: Q: What happens if a Redis single-threaded command takes 500ms (e.g. KEYS *)?
cards.question: Q: What happens if a Redis single-threaded command takes 500ms (e.g. KEYS *)?
cards.answer_30s: A: Every other client connection queues up behind that command, causing cluster-wide latency spikes and health-check timeouts. Replace `KEYS *` with cursor-based `SCAN 0 MATCH prefix:* COUNT 100`, break huge `DEL` into `UNLINK` (async background free), and monitor `SLOWLOG`.

code.body: UNLINK huge_set_key  # Non-blocking async memory reclamation

cards.typical_use: Preventing self-inflicted production outages in Redis.
pitfalls: UNLINK vs DEL is a great practical tip—UNLINK removes the key reference in O(1) and frees memory on a background thread.

cards.title: Q: How do you handle hot keys in a Redis Cluster?
cards.question: Q: How do you handle hot keys in a Redis Cluster?
cards.answer_30s: A: A single hot key hashes to one shard, saturating its CPU/NIC. Mitigate by: 1) Adding a small in-process local cache (L1) in app pods with 1-5s TTL, 2) Replicating the hot key across N shards (`key#1..#N`) and reading a random replica, or 3) Using Redis 6 client-side tracking.
cards.typical_use: Solving skewed traffic bottlenecks in distributed caching.
pitfalls: L1 in-memory cache + L2 Redis is the standard multi-tier caching pattern.
